query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In an equiatomic FeCoNi film, incorporating approximately 15 at.% Pt (validated by DFT to retain configurational entropy above 1.0R) followed by RTA at ~700°C for 30 s will induce partial L1₀-like chemical ordering that increases coercivity by at least one order of magnitude compared to the as-deposited fcc film.
generation.material_initial_state: Sputtered, equiatomic FeCoNi thin film with a disordered fcc structure and low coercivity (~10 Oe baseline).
generation.intervention: Introduce ~15 at.% Pt into the FeCoNi alloy during sputtering and subsequently subject the film to a rapid thermal annealing process.
generation.conditions: Annealing at approximately 700°C for 30 seconds in an inert atmosphere, with process parameters chosen to avoid oxidation and ensure uniform Pt distribution.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a partially ordered L1₀-like tetragonal phase within the predominantly high-entropy matrix.
generation.mechanism: Pt atoms, through strong spin–orbit coupling and their effect on local bonding, reduce the cubic lattice symmetry and enhance magnetocrystalline anisotropy. This increased anisotropy improves domain wall pinning, thereby boosting coercivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: A coercivity increase by at least 10× (e.g., from ~10 Oe to ~100 Oe or more) while retaining high saturation magnetization; the L1₀-like ordering should be observable via XRD as superlattice reflections.
generation.baseline: As-deposited equiatomic FeCoNi film with a chemically disordered fcc structure and low coercivity.
generation.boundary: Pt additions must be kept within a narrow window (approximately 10–20 at.%) to maintain high configurational entropy; excessive Pt (>20 at.%) may lead to multiphase precipitation.
generation.uncertainty: While initial calculations support the chosen Pt content and RTA parameters, variations in film thickness and deposition uniformity may affect the degree of ordering and coercivity enhancement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of sputtered equiatomic FeCoNi films with Pt contents varied around 15 at.% (e.g., 10, 15, and 20 at.%) and subject them to RTA at 700°C for 30 s. Use XRD to detect the emergence of L1₀ ordering and measure magnetic hysteresis loops using VSM.
measurements: XRD peak splitting or superlattice reflections indicative of L1₀ ordering
Coercivity (Hc) obtained from magnetic hysteresis loops
Saturation magnetization (Ms) to ensure minimal degradation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If XRD does not reveal low-symmetry ordering or if the measured coercivity does not increase by at least 10× relative to the baseline film, or if configurational entropy calculations indicate <1.0R, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Certain HEA compositions may exhibit long‐range chemical order through the emergence of multiple sublattices, analogous to high entropy ceramics,[  ] leading to so‐called “high entropy intermetallic” (HEI) compounds.[  ] Previously, transition metal alloys with high anisotropy, such as the L10 phases of FePt and FePd have been achieved by annealing of equiatomic solid solution pre‐cursors.[  ] In the case of metastable high anisotropy phases such as L10 FeNi, unconventional annealing techniques have been employed.[  ] In particular, rapid thermal annealing (RTA) of transition metal alloy films on Si/SiO2 is an effective means of inducing high anisotropy phase formation in solid solution precursors, in part due to the substrate‐induced strain.[  ] In this study, we experimentally demonstrate two thin film HEAs with large coercivity and magnetic anisotropy achieved by RTA. We show that RTA treatment of equiatomic FeCoNiMnCu thin films leads to ≈40‐fold increase in coercivity. By introduction of 50 at.% Pt, we realize an L10 HEI phase of (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy resulting from a reduced lattice symmetry and strong spin‐orbit coupling. A significant increas

While the combination of saturation magnetization and coercivity for these RTA‐ treated FeCoNiMnCu films is impressive in comparison to previously reported bulk systems, the coercivity is still modest, due to the high symmetry of the cubic lattice which limits the intrinsic magnetocrystalline anisotropy. The facilitation of low‐symmetry chemical order and crystal structure combined with strong spin‐orbit coupling is in general necessary to realize strong magnetocrysalline anisotropy. To achieve these conditions in a high entropy system, we have added 50 at.% Pt to the FeCoNiMnCu alloy, employing the high entropy intermetallic design approach in search of highly anisotropic L10 ordering. Although the certainty of Pt sites reduces the configurational entropy compared to the equiatomic case, we demonstrate below that such optimized entropy can still stabilize a single high‐entropy L10 phase.

In summary, we have achieved high magnetic anisotropy in rare‐earth‐free high entropy metallic thin films by sputtering and RTA. Robust magnetic order of both fcc FeCoNiMnCu and L10 (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt films has been demonstrated. The FeCoNiMnCu films exhibit a large coercivity increase after RTA, resulting from microstructural changes and strain‐induced anisotropy enhancement which strengthens domain wall pinning. Addition of Pt reduces the symmetry of the cubic fcc lattice to an intermetallic tetragonal L10 phase of (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt. Although the Pt insertion lowers the configurational entropy compared to the equiatomic case, the entropy is still high enough to stabilize an L10 single phase. This intermetallic phase is confirmed to host high magnetocrystalline anisotropy, likely attributed to the lower symmetry of the L10 structure and the strong spin‐orbit coupling provided by the Pt insertion. These findings demonstrate the promise of high‐entropy intermetallic design as a key avenue to search for new high‐entropy magnets beyond the equiatomic composition.

papers.title: Single-Phase L1₀-Ordered High Entropy Thin Films with High Magnetic Anisotropy.
papers.approach: Sputtered equiatomic films on Si/SiO₂ substrates followed by rapid thermal annealing (RTA) to induce a phase transformation. A 50 at.% Pt addition was used to trigger L1₀ ordering.
papers.findings: The RTA-treated FeCoNiMnCu films exhibited an approximately 40-fold increase in coercivity relative to as-grown films. With the addition of Pt, an L1₀ high entropy intermetallic phase formed, leading to a three orders of magnitude increase in coercivity along with enhanced magnetic anisotropy.
papers.mechanism: Pt incorporation reduces the lattice symmetry from the high-symmetry fcc phase to a tetragonal L1₀ structure. This symmetry reduction, combined with strong spin–orbit coupling from Pt and strain-induced anisotropy (from rapid thermal processing), enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy and improves domain wall pinning.

established: Transition metal high-entropy alloys can undergo phase transitions via RTA, where microstructural evolution (including strain-induced anisotropy) can significantly increase coercivity.
Chemical ordering, in particular the formation of L1₀ or similar low-symmetry intermetallic phases, enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
Incorporation of heavy elements like Pt—which have strong spin–orbit coupling—can induce such ordering while still maintaining a high enough configurational entropy (≥1.0R) for high-entropy behavior.

approaches_tried.approach: Rapid Thermal Annealing (RTA) on sputtered equiatomic FeCoNiMnCu films
approaches_tried.outcome: Approximately 40-fold increase in coercivity compared to as-deposited samples, due to microstructural evolution and strain-induced anisotropy.

approaches_tried.approach: Insertion of 50 at.% Pt into the FeCoNiMnCu alloy to promote L1₀ ordering
approaches_tried.outcome: Formation of a low-symmetry tetragonal L1₀ phase with a three orders of magnitude enhancement in coercivity and high magnetic anisotropy.

mechanisms: The transition from a high-symmetry fcc structure to a low-symmetry ordered intermetallic (L1₀) structure increases intrinsic magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
Strong spin–orbit coupling provided by Pt enhances the pinning of magnetic domain walls.
Strain induced during RTA further promotes lattice distortions that aid in coercivity enhancement.
disagreements: While some studies attribute coercivity enhancement primarily to strain-induced anisotropy and grain distortions from RTA, others emphasize that chemical ordering (via heavy element addition) is the dominant factor.
There remains debate on the optimal balance between configurational entropy (which favors disordered soft magnetic phases) and the degree of ordering needed to achieve high coercivity.
open_questions: Can the Pt-induced L1₀ ordering intervention be successfully applied directly to simpler or more limited FeCoNi-based systems (without Mn/Cu additions) while still maintaining the required high configurational entropy?
What are the precise processing parameters (e.g., annealing temperature, time, substrate-induced strain) that optimize the transformation to a hard magnetic L1₀ phase in these systems?
How robust is the coercivity enhancement across varying film thicknesses and under different thermal conditions, and what trade-offs exist with saturation magnetization?
opportunities: Investigate the effect of controlled Pt additions in a nearly equiatomic FeCoNi system to induce L1₀ ordering while ensuring the configurational entropy remains at or above 1.0R.
Systematically explore RTA parameters (temperature, duration, substrate influence) to fine-tune the phase transformation and maximize coercivity.

Combine heavy-metal induced ordering with strain engineering to achieve an optimal balance of high coercivity and saturation magnetization, potentially creating new classes of high-entropy permanent magnets.

directions.direction: Alloy composition design via minor heavy‐element addition to induce chemical ordering.
directions.assessment: Adding a small fraction of a heavy element (e.g. Pt or Pd) is known to reduce lattice symmetry via strong spin–orbit coupling and trigger L1₀ ordering. Such ordering enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy, which is directly related to increased coercivity. Evidence supports that Pt addition in similar HEA systems (even though with additional elements) produces dramatic coercivity increases (PMC11426066::web::019::conclusion, PMC11426066::web::012::results_and_discussion). This intervention meets configurational entropy constraints if the heavy element content is kept at a minor level.

directions.direction: Optimized rapid thermal annealing (RTA) parameters to drive ordering and strain.
directions.assessment: RTA is shown to trigger phase transitions via strain‐induced anisotropy and can promote low‐symmetry ordering, as evidenced by a 40‐fold coercivity increase in untreated films (PMC11426066::web::000::abstract). Adjusting RTA temperature and duration can potentially drive more complete ordering in an equiatomic FeCoNi alloy, thereby increasing coercivity. This approach addresses microstructure directly while preserving high entropy.

directions.direction: Substrate‐induced strain engineering in thin film deposition.
directions.assessment: Depositing the alloy on a lattice‐mismatched substrate can introduce anisotropic strain that may distort the cubic fcc structure and potentially stimulate chemical ordering or domain wall pinning. Such approaches have led to coercivity enhancements in other systems. It directly targets the low coercivity limitation while keeping the composition near equiatomic.

directions.direction: Thermomechanical treatment combining severe plastic deformation with thermal annealing.
directions.assessment: Introducing a deformation step (e.g. high pressure torsion type process) before or after RTA can refine the grain structure and generate nanodomains with enhanced domain wall pinning. This dual intervention, while still considered a single processing approach, directly attacks the soft magnetic behavior by enhancing microstructural defects and anisotropy without substantially altering the overall equiatomic composition.
